claims.text: Optimizing lamellar spacing in eutectic high-entropy alloys will simultaneously increase yield strength and ductility relative to the standard cast microstructure.
Conventional casting can produce eutectic high-entropy alloys with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure.
The conventionally cast lamellae are evenly or uniformly spaced.
Controlled heat treatment or thermomechanical processing can coarsen or introduce a gentle gradient in lamellar spacing without changing the overall phase composition.
The proposed benefit should occur at room temperature under quasi-static mechanical loading.
Lamellar spacing and its gradient dictate phase connectivity and interface characteristics.
Alternating soft fcc and hard bcc/B2 phases are a design feature of eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Optimized lamellar spacing improves the balance between load transfer and dislocation mobility.
Sufficient phase boundaries impede crack initiation while preserving plasticity in softer domains.
A tailored lamellar architecture retards crack propagation and improves stress distribution.
Fine lamellar fcc/B2 eutectic microstructures can exhibit a combination of high fracture strength and high tensile ductility at room temperature.
The treated alloy will have higher yield strength than the baseline cast alloy.
The treated alloy will have greater ductility than the baseline cast alloy.
The magnitude of improvement depends on alloy composition and processing.
The benefit may be limited to alloys that naturally form a two-phase eutectic structure.
Excessive coarsening or loss of phase integrity could degrade mechanical properties.
Optimal lamellar spacing values depend on the specific alloy composition and processing parameters.
Reproducibility at scale and across different compositions may be challenging.
